title: Background check delays for recruiters on Mac: causes, costs and fixes for 2026
metaTitle: Background check delays: causes, costs and fixes for recruiters
description: Background check delays slow every hire. Here is why they happen, what they cost, and free fixes recruiters on a Mac can use this week.
intro: Background check delays happen when the check starts late, when records need manual review, or when a school or county search takes longer than expected. The cost shows up as open roles, cold candidates and recruiter time spent chasing status. This page covers the causes, the real costs, and fixes you can use without buying anything.
tldr: Delays often start with timing. The check may start after the offer, and everything waits behind it.
Checkr lists $29.99 to $94.99 per report, and county searches and court fees add to that.
Track each file in one sheet, send status updates on a schedule, and ask your vendor for turnaround in writing.
Lazur can draft the update, dictate notes and explain your screen out loud. It cannot run the check for you.

blocks.text: Why background check delays matter in 2026

Hiring is slow for many reasons, and checks are only one of them. The BLS reported 7.5 million job openings and a 3.4% hires rate for September 2026. That is about 5.4 million hires in one month, and candidates have choices.

A slow check holds a file open while the candidate keeps looking. The delay is easy to ignore on a report. It is hard to ignore when the offer goes to someone else. Treat the check as part of the hiring plan, not a box at the end.
What a background check delay costs you

The direct fees are easy to find. Checkr lists its per-report packages at $29.99 for Basic, $59.99 for Essential and $94.99 for Complete. Enterprise pricing is custom. Checkr's pricing page also says 97% of its customers find its turnaround faster than the competition. It names no competitor and no time frame, so treat that line as marketing.

blocks.caption: Checkr list prices as published on its pricing page, accessed 2026-11-09.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example at list prices. Take one Essential package and add one county criminal search and two verifications. The total is $59.99 + $25 + $12.50 + $12.50, or $110. Court and database fees can pass through at cost on top, so the final bill can be higher than the quote.
Measure your own delay before you change anything

Do not guess how long your checks take. Measure them first. Open Google Sheets in Chrome, create a sheet, and set up seven columns: candidate, role, check ordered, consent received, result received, days open and next follow-up. Put real dates in the three date columns.

In F2, the days open column, type =IF(E2="",TODAY()-D2,E2-D2). Drag it down. A finished check shows the days it took. A check still running shows the days it has waited so far, and the number rises each day. Set column F to Format > Number > Number so it shows days, not dates.

After a few weeks, sort by days open, largest first. Use Data > Create a filter, then sort column F. The slowest rows show where your process stalls. Look for patterns, such as consent that sits for days before the check starts. For sorting steps, read the [sort guide](/how-to/sort-data-by-column-in-google-sheets).
Keep candidate names out of shared links. Keep the sheet inside the tools your team has approved for candidate records.
A good status note is short. It answers three questions, and it never reveals what the check found.

items: The status: in progress, waiting on a step, or complete.
The next date you expect to hear something.
The person the candidate can contact with a question.
A reminder that the candidate can ask about the process through the proper channel.

blocks.text: Mistakes that stretch a background check
The first mistake is silence. A candidate who hears nothing for a week may assume the worst. Send one note when the check starts and another when it finishes or stalls.

The second mistake is calling the vendor every day. A daily call rarely moves a file that waits on a county or a school. Ask for an update on a fixed day. Write down the answer and the name of the person who gave it.
The third mistake is ordering checks for candidates who are unlikely to get an offer. You pay per report, and the vendor does the work for nothing in return. Narrow the list before you order.
When a report comes back with a problem
Errors happen, so plan for a dispute. Do not argue a record from memory. Ask the candidate for any court or agency paperwork they hold. Then send the dispute to the vendor in writing and keep a copy.

The FTC says a post-adverse action notice must name the consumer reporting company. It must say the company did not make the decision, and it must tell the candidate of the right to dispute inaccuracies. Use that as your checklist for what the candidate must receive.
Candidate data and regulated roles
Background reports hold personal information. Follow your employer's rules on candidate data before you copy anything from a report into any tool, including an AI assistant.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold ⌥⌘. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your employer may still ban AI tools for candidate files, so check first.
If you recruit for nursing, law or accounting, rules for client or patient data may apply to the same file. Ask your compliance lead before you use any AI tool near those records.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur does not click buttons, log into a vendor portal or start a check. It helps with the writing, the explaining and the reading around the process. That covers the time you lose to status notes and to hunting for answers.

Ask it to draft the candidate update in Gmail, then dictate notes into your tracker with fn. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask what a vendor status word means. It answers out loud. It can circle the button you need, but you do the click.

Research jobs run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and come back with a summary and a report. Use that to collect vendor pricing and turnaround pages you have not read yet. Then check each figure on the page yourself.
Read the rules before you change the process

Law sets the floor, and your employer sets the rest. The Fair Credit Reporting Act requires a copy of the report and a written summary of rights before an adverse action. It sets no waiting period in days, so any waiting period is policy.
Read 15 U.S. Code § 1681b on Cornell's site and the FTC's employer guide. Then ask HR or counsel what your company requires before you change the order of steps or the timing of checks.
Next steps this week

Start with the tracker. Measure the checks you closed last month, then pick one change to test on the next few roles. Compare days open after a full round, not after one candidate. Numbers from your own sheet give HR a clearer case than a guess.

faq.question: How long does a background check take?
faq.answer: No source I opened gives a measured turnaround time, so no single number is safe to quote. Ask your vendor for its median by package, in writing. Track your own days open for a month to get your number.

faq.question: Does the law set a waiting period before rejecting a candidate?
faq.answer: No. The Fair Credit Reporting Act requires a copy of the report and a summary of rights before an adverse action. It sets no number of days to wait. Any waiting period comes from your employer's policy, so check with HR or counsel.

faq.question: Can I start a background check before the interview?
faq.answer: Check your employer's policy and get written consent first. Starting early can save time. Ordering checks for candidates who are unlikely to get an offer wastes money, so keep the list short.

faq.question: Why does my vendor say the file is still pending?
faq.answer: A pending file usually waits on something. That can be consent, a county search, a school or a former employer. Ask the vendor which step holds the file and the date it expects that step to finish.

faq.question: Can Lazur run the background check for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or log into vendor portals. It can draft the candidate update, dictate notes, explain what is on your screen and guide you through each step.

faq.question: Is it safe to use an AI assistant near candidate data?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: What do Checkr's list prices cover?
faq.answer: Checkr lists packages at $29.99, $59.99 and $94.99 per report. County criminal searches cost $25 plus court fees, and verifications start at $12.50 each. Check the pricing page for current terms.

costs.title: Direct fees add up fast
costs.text: Checkr lists $29.99 to $94.99 per report, county criminal searches at $25 plus court fees, and verifications from $12.50 each. Third-party court and database fees may pass through at cost, so the final bill can run above the quote.

costs.title: Open roles stay open
costs.text: Each extra day a role stays open is a day your team covers the work. The BLS reported 7.5 million job openings for September 2026, so candidates have plenty of options.

costs.title: Candidates take other offers
costs.text: A candidate waiting on a check may accept another offer before your result arrives. The BLS hires rate was 3.4% in September 2026, so replacing a lost candidate takes time.

costs.title: Recruiter hours go to chasing
costs.text: Status chases and repeated vendor calls take time from sourcing and interviews. No source I checked measures these hours, so log them in your sheet for a month to find your own number.

causes.title: The check starts too late
causes.text: Some teams order the check after the final interview or after the offer is signed. That puts the wait on the critical path, so the start date slips while the check runs. The problem is worst when the offer is out and the candidate is waiting on paperwork. No study I opened shows how much earlier starts shorten time to hire, so treat timing as a test, not a proven fix.

causes.title: Records do not match the candidate
causes.text: Criminal records do not always agree across sources. In a Criminology study by Lageson and Stewart, 101 people with at least one criminal charge had state reports compared with private background checks. Of those, 60% had at least one false-positive error on a regulated check, and 50% on an unregulated one. 90% and 92% had at least one false-negative error. Each mismatch can trigger a review and a dispute. The sample is small, so it does not predict every check.

causes.title: County and court lookups are separate steps
causes.text: A county criminal search is a separate lookup, and court fees come on top. Third-party court and database fees may pass through at cost, which means one file can touch more than one source. Each extra lookup is another place the file can wait. None of the pages I opened gives a turnaround time for these steps, so ask your vendor for its own numbers.

causes.title: Education and employment checks wait on other offices
causes.text: Education and employment checks ask a school or a former employer to answer. The school side can be fast when a verification service covers it, but a school outside that coverage can still hold the file. A former employer who does not reply stops the check until someone follows up.

causes.title: The notice step adds time
causes.text: Before an adverse action based on a consumer report, the Fair Credit Reporting Act requires you to send a copy of the report and a written summary of rights. The statute sets no waiting period. A team without a written process for that notice tends to lose track of it, and the file waits while everyone assumes someone else sent it.

causes.title: The candidate has not finished the forms
causes.text: A check cannot start until the candidate gives consent and completes the vendor's forms. An unopened email can hold a file for days. Nobody notices until someone asks where the file is.

fixes.title: Collect consent at the first allowed point
fixes.text: Move consent to the earliest stage your policy allows. Ask the candidate to sign the authorization when they accept the interview, if HR permits that. Each day saved here is a day the candidate does not spend waiting in silence. Confirm the timing with HR first, since your employer sets the policy.

fixes.title: Order parallel checks in one request
fixes.text: Order criminal, employment and education checks in one request, not one after another. Ask your vendor whether it runs them in parallel. No source I opened measures how much this saves, so test it on a few files and compare the days open column.

fixes.title: Track every file in one sheet
fixes.text: Put every open check in one sheet with a days open column. Sort by that column every week and chase the oldest files first. The measurement steps above show the formula to use.

fixes.title: Send status updates on a schedule
fixes.text: Send each candidate a short update on a fixed day until the result arrives. In Gmail on the web, click the arrow next to Send and choose Schedule send, so the note goes out on time even when you are in meetings. See the [scheduling guide](/how-to/schedule-an-email-to-send-later-in-gmail).

fixes.title: Get turnaround in writing from your vendor
fixes.text: Ask for the median time for each package you buy, measured over the last few months, and ask for it in writing. Ignore marketing lines like the one on Checkr's pricing page. A useful answer names a number and the conditions behind it.

fixes.title: Use the ATS integration if you have one
fixes.text: Greenhouse lists 24 partner background-check integrations, including Checkr, HireRight and Accurate. If your ATS has one, order the check from the candidate record so the status stays in one place. Greenhouse's support page does not say how checks start or how long they take, so confirm the flow with your admin.

fixes.title: Name one owner for every open check
fixes.text: Write an owner's name next to every open check in the tracker. A file with no owner gets no chase, and it stalls. Make the owner the person who sends the candidate update each week.

fixes.title: Check whether the school route is instant
fixes.text: The National Student Clearinghouse says employers can immediately verify enrollment and graduation information from most U.S. colleges and universities. Ask your vendor whether education checks use that route. For schools outside that coverage, ask for the vendor's own path and expected timing.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Measure last month's checks
plan.text: Open a Google Sheets file in Chrome. Add the seven columns from the measurement section. Fill in dates for every check you closed last month, so you have a baseline.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Find the slowest stage
plan.text: Sort the days open column from largest to smallest. Note which stage each slow file is stuck in: consent, vendor, county or notice. Count stages, not candidates, to see the pattern.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Write one status note template
plan.text: Draft a status update in Gmail with Lazur, then save it as a template. Keep the note short, with a status line, a next date and a contact name.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Ask the vendor in writing
plan.text: Email your vendor and ask for median turnaround by package, measured over the last few months. Ask which steps run in parallel and which wait on a county or school.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Pick one timing change
plan.text: Choose one change, usually collecting consent earlier, and apply it to the next roles that qualify. Log days open for each one. Compare results after a full round, not after one candidate.

plan.label: Week 2
plan.title: Review the numbers with HR
plan.text: Bring the sheet to your HR or compliance lead. Confirm the timing change matches your employer's policy before it goes live. Then decide whether to keep it.
